title: The House of Finwë (family line)
kind: Family line of the Noldor kings
blurb: The descendants of Finwë, first king of the Noldor, through Fëanor, Fingolfin and Finarfin.
book:
Finwë led the Noldor from Cuiviénen to Valinor and ruled them at Tirion. His line holds all the royal houses of the Noldor.

Finwë, first king of the Noldor, slain by Morgoth at Formenos
First marriage, to Míriel: Fëanor
Fëanor and Nerdanel had seven sons: Maedhros, Maglor, Celegorm, Caranthir, Curufin, Amrod, Amras
Curufin's son: Celebrimbor, maker of the Three Rings
Second marriage, to Indis of the Vanyar: Fingolfin and Finarfin
Fingolfin's children: Fingon, Turgon, Aredhel
Fingon's son: Gil-galad, last High King of the Noldor
Turgon's daughter: Idril, wife of Tuor, mother of Eärendil
Aredhel and Eöl: Maeglin
Finarfin's children: Finrod Felagund, Orodreth, Angrod, Aegnor, Galadriel
Orodreth's daughter: Finduilas
Galadriel and Celeborn: Celebrían, wife of Elrond

The list follows the published Silmarillion. Tolkien's later notes differ on some points. They add daughters of Finwë and Indis, Findis and Írimë, and a fourth child of Fingolfin, Argon. They also make Orodreth a son of Angrod, and Gil-galad a son of Orodreth rather than of Fingon.
sources: The Silmarillion, chapters 1, 5, 6 and 13
The Silmarillion, genealogical tables

title: The House of Bëor (family line)
kind: Family line of the First House of Men
blurb: Bëor led the first Men to enter Beleriand. His house gave Beren, Dior and, through Elwing, the line of Elrond.
book:
Bëor the Old led the first Men over the Blue Mountains. His people became friends of Finrod Felagund and held Dorthonion for many years.

Bëor the Old, first lord of the house, who served Finrod
Baran, elder son of Bëor
Boron, son of Baran
Boromir, son of Boron
Bregor, son of Boromir, father of Bregolas and Barahir
Bregolas, lord of the house, slain in the Dagor Bragollach
Bregolas's sons: Baragund and Belegund
Baragund's daughter: Morwen, wife of Húrin of the House of Hador
Belegund's daughter: Rían, wife of Huor, mother of Tuor
Barahir, brother of Bregolas, who received the Ring of Barahir from Finrod
Barahir's son: Beren, who won the Silmaril with Lúthien
Beren and Lúthien: Dior Eluchíl, called the Heir of Thingol
Dior and Nimloth: Elwing, Eluréd and Elurín
Elwing and Eärendil: Elrond and Elros

This list follows the main line of lords. It leaves out many other members of the house, such as the daughters of Bregor and the kin of Andreth.
sources: The Silmarillion, chapters 17 and 18
The Silmarillion, genealogical tables

title: The House of Hador (family line)
kind: Family line of the Third House of Men
blurb: The line of Hador Lórindol, lord of Dor-lómin, from which came Húrin, Túrin, Tuor and Eärendil.
book:
Hador Lórindol was given the land of Dor-lómin by Fingolfin. His people were tall and fair, and many were golden-haired.

Hador Lórindol, lord of Dor-lómin, slain at Eithel Sirion in the Dagor Bragollach
Galdor the Tall, son of Hador, who succeeded him
Gundor, younger son of Hador, slain beside his father
Glóredhel, daughter of Hador, wife of Haldir of the Haladin
Galdor's children: Húrin and Huor, with Rían as Huor's wife
Galdor's wife: Hareth, of the House of Haleth
Húrin and Morwen: Túrin, Urwen called Lalaith, and Nienor
Huor and Rían: Tuor
Tuor and Idril: Eärendil
Eärendil and Elwing: Elrond and Elros

Through Tuor the house joined the lines of Thingol and Finwë. Through Elros and Elrond it passed down to the Kings of Númenor and the Dúnedain.

places.note: Hador and his heirs held Dor-lómin as lords under the High King.

sources: The Silmarillion, chapters 17, 18, 20 and 21

title: The House of Haleth (family line)
kind: Family line of the Haladin
blurb: The people of Haleth, who lived in the forest of Brethil, and their lords down to Brandir.
book:
The Haladin were a smaller people of Men. They lived apart in the forest of Brethil and were led for a time by a woman, Haleth.

Haldad, father of Haleth, slain by Orcs
Haldar, brother of Haleth, slain with him
Haleth, the lady who led the Haladin into Brethil
Haldan, son of Haldar and nephew of Haleth, who ruled after her; Haleth had no children
Halmir, son of Haldan
Halmir's daughter: Hareth, wife of Galdor of the House of Hador and mother of Húrin and Huor
Haldir, son of Halmir, husband of Glóredhel of the House of Hador, slain in the Nírnaeth Arnoediad
Handir, son of Haldir, slain in battle with Orcs
Brandir the Lame, son of Handir, last lord of the house
Hunthor, a kinsman of Brandir but not a lord, killed by a falling stone at Cabed-en-Aras

The Silmarillion names these lords in this order. It does not say who led the Haladin after Brandir died.

places.note: Ephel Brandir was the hidden stronghold of the Haladin in Brethil.

sources: The Silmarillion, chapters 17, 18 and 21
Unfinished Tales, Part Two

title: From Thingol and Melian to Elrond and Arwen (family line)
kind: Line of the Half-elven
blurb: The line from the Elven-king Thingol and the Maia Melian down to Elrond, Arwen and Aragorn, with the line of Tuor and Idril that joins it.
book:
This line joins Elves, Men and a Maia. It runs from Doriath through Beren and Lúthien to the Half-elven of the Second and Third Ages.

Thingol and Melian (a Maia): Lúthien
Lúthien and Beren: Dior
Dior and Nimloth: Elwing (and her brothers Eluréd and Elurín)
Tuor of the House of Hador and Idril, daughter of Turgon: Eärendil
Eärendil and Elwing: Elrond and Elros
Elros became the first King of Númenor
Elrond and Celebrían: Elladan, Elrohir and Arwen
Arwen and Aragorn: Eldarion and daughters

Elrond's mother Elwing came from Doriath. His father Eärendil came from Gondolin and from the House of Hador. Elrond and Elros chose different fates: Elros chose mortality and Elrond chose to remain among the Elves. Arwen later chose the fate of Men.

facts.Chosen fate: Elros chose Men; Elrond chose Elves; Arwen chose Men

places.note: Menegroth was the hall of Thingol and Melian in Doriath.
Rivendell was the house of Elrond in the Second and Third Ages.

sources: The Silmarillion, chapters 19, 23 and 24
The Lord of the Rings, Appendix A and Appendix B

title: The Kings and Queens of Númenor (list)
kind: List of rulers of Númenor
blurb: The twenty-five rulers of Númenor, in order, from Elros to Ar-Pharazôn, with the rightful queen Tar-Míriel.
book:
Elros, son of Eärendil, founded the kingdom of Númenor in S.A. 32. The sceptre passed from parent to eldest child, and after a change of the law under Tar-Aldarion the eldest child could inherit, whether son or daughter.

1. Elros Tar-Minyatur (S.A. 32 to 442)
2. Vardamir Nólimon
3. Tar-Amandil
4. Tar-Elendil
5. Tar-Meneldur
6. Tar-Aldarion
7. Tar-Ancalimë, the first ruling Queen
8. Tar-Anárion
9. Tar-Súrion
10. Tar-Telperiën, the second ruling Queen
11. Tar-Minastir
12. Tar-Ciryatan
13. Tar-Atanamir the Great
14. Tar-Ancalimon
15. Tar-Telemmaitë
16. Tar-Vanimeldë, the third ruling Queen
17. Tar-Alcarin
18. Tar-Calmacil
19. Tar-Ardamin
20. Ar-Adûnakhôr
21. Ar-Zimrathôn
22. Ar-Sakalthôr
23. Ar-Gimilzôr
24. Tar-Palantír, who also bore the name Ar-Inziladûn
25. Ar-Pharazôn the Golden, who seized the sceptre in S.A. 3255 by forcing Tar-Míriel, daughter of Tar-Palantír and the rightful heir, to marry him

Ar-Pharazôn brought about the Downfall in S.A. 3319. This numbering follows Unfinished Tales. Appendix A leaves out Tar-Ardamin, so its count differs by one. Vardamir is counted as king but gave the sceptre at once to his son. From Ar-Adûnakhôr on, the kings took Adûnaic names and grew hostile to the Valar.
sources: The Silmarillion, Akallabêth
The Lord of the Rings, Appendix A (I)
Unfinished Tales, Part Two

title: The Lords of Andúnië (list)
kind: Partial list of the Lords of Andúnië
blurb: The Lords of Andúnië, who were kin to the Kings of Númenor and leaders of the Faithful, and ended with Amandil and Elendil.
book:
Andúnië lay on the west coast of Númenor. Its lords were of the line of Elros and were friends of the Elves.

Valandil, first Lord of Andúnië, son of Silmariën, eldest child of Tar-Elendil, and of Elatan of Andúnië
A long line of lords followed him. The books name few of them. Inzilbêth, mother of Tar-Palantír, came of this house
Amandil, last Lord of Andúnië before the Downfall
Elendil, son of Amandil, leader of the Faithful and later High King of the Dúnedain in exile
Isildur and Anárion, sons of Elendil

Silmariën was the eldest child of Tar-Elendil, but the law of that time let only a son inherit, so her brother Meneldur received the sceptre. For that reason her line stayed among the lords. Late in Númenor the Kings turned against the Valar, and the lords became the leaders of the Faithful. They were later made to leave Andúnië and live at Rómenna. Amandil sailed west to plead with the Valar and was not seen again. Elendil escaped the Downfall with his sons and founded Arnor and Gondor. This list is not complete.
sources: The Silmarillion, Akallabêth
Unfinished Tales, Part Two, chapter 1

title: The High Kings of the Noldor (list)
kind: List of the Noldor's High Kings
blurb: The kings who held the title of High King of the Noldor, from Finwë to Gil-galad.
book:
After Finwë died, the kingship of the Noldor passed through the house of Finwë. In Middle-earth the title went to Fingolfin's line.

Finwë, king in Valinor, slain by Morgoth at Formenos
Fëanor, who led the Noldor to Middle-earth and fell soon after the landing
Maedhros, heir of Fëanor, who gave up the kingship to Fingolfin
Fingolfin, High King of the Noldor (died in his duel with Morgoth soon after the Dagor Bragollach of F.A. 455; the later annals give F.A. 456)
Fingon, son of Fingolfin (slain in the Nírnaeth Arnoediad, F.A. 472)
Turgon, brother of Fingon, King of Gondolin (died when Gondolin fell, F.A. 510 in the later annals)
Gil-galad, High King in Lindon (slain in the Last Alliance, S.A. 3441)

Maedhros was the eldest of Fëanor's sons, but he gave up his claim. Finarfin ruled the Noldor who stayed in Aman. The Silmarillion calls Gil-galad a son of Fingon; Tolkien's later notes make him a son of Orodreth. Some of the Noldor lived outside the realm of the High King, such as those in Nargothrond.

places.note: Turgon ruled the hidden city of Gondolin and became High King after Fingon fell.
Fingolfin and Fingon held Hithlum as High Kings.

sources: The Silmarillion, chapters 6, 13, 18, 20, 23 and 24

title: The Kings of Arnor and Arthedain (list)
kind: List of the northern Dúnedain kings
blurb: The kings of Arnor from Elendil to Eärendur, and of Arthedain from Amlaith to Arvedui.
book:
Elendil founded Arnor in S.A. 3320. After the death of Eärendur in T.A. 861 the realm split into Arthedain, Cardolan and Rhudaur.

Elendil the Tall (slain in S.A. 3441)
Isildur (slain in the Gladden Fields, T.A. 2)
Valandil
Eldacar
Arantar
Tarcil
Tarondor
Valandur
Elendur
Eärendur, last king of undivided Arnor (T.A. 861)
Arthedain: Amlaith of Fornost
Beleg
Mallor
Celepharn
Celebrindor
Malvegil
Argeleb I (slain in the war with Rhudaur)
Arveleg I
Araphor
Argeleb II
Arvegil
Arveleg II
Araval
Araphant
Arvedui, last king, drowned in the Ice Bay of Forochel (T.A. 1975)

Arvedui claimed the crown of Gondor as well. His son Aranarth became the first Chieftain of the Dúnedain. Aragorn later reunited both kingdoms.

places.note: Annúminas was the first capital of Arnor.
Fornost Erain became the seat of the kings of Arthedain.

sources: The Lord of the Rings, Appendix A (I, iii)
The Silmarillion, Of the Rings of Power

title: The Chieftains of the Dúnedain (list)
kind: List of the heirs of Isildur in the North
blurb: The Chieftains of the Dúnedain of the North, from Aranarth to Aragorn II, in order.
book:
After Arvedui was lost, the heirs of Isildur kept the title of Chieftain. They lived in secret and guarded the North, with the heirlooms kept at Rivendell.

Aranarth, son of Arvedui (T.A. 1975)
Arahael
Aranuir
Aravir
Aragorn I (slain by wolves)
Araglas
Arahad I
Aragost
Aravorn
Arahad II
Arassuil
Arathorn I
Argonui
Arador (slain by hill-trolls, T.A. 2930)
Arathorn II, husband of Gilraen (slain by Orcs, T.A. 2933)
Aragorn II Elessar, born T.A. 2931

Aragorn was two years old when his father died. His mother took him to Rivendell, where Elrond raised him. He became Chieftain at once and later became King of the Reunited Kingdom.

places.note: The heirlooms of the line were held at Rivendell by Elrond.

sources: The Lord of the Rings, Appendix A (I, iii)

title: The Kings of Gondor (list)
kind: List of the Kings of Gondor
blurb: The kings of Gondor in order, from Anárion and Isildur to Eärnur, with Aragorn restoring the line.
book:
Gondor was founded in S.A. 3320 by Isildur and Anárion. After Isildur left for the north, the line of Anárion held the crown.

Elendil, High King of Arnor and Gondor
Isildur and Anárion, joint rulers
Meneldil, son of Anárion
Cemendur
Eärendil
Anardil
Ostoher
Rómendacil I (Tarostar)
Turambar
Atanatar I
Siriondil
Tarannon Falastur, first of the ship-kings
Eärnil I
Ciryandil
Hyarmendacil I (Ciryaher)
Atanatar II Alcarin
Narmacil I
Calmacil
Minalcar, regent, later Rómendacil II
Valacar
Eldacar (Vinitharya)
Castamir the Usurper
Eldacar, restored
Aldamir
Hyarmendacil II (Vinyarion)
Minardil
Telemnar
Tarondor
Telumehtar Umbardacil
Narmacil II
Calimehtar
Ondoher
Eärnil II
Eärnur, last king (vanished in T.A. 2050)

The Ruling Stewards held the city after Eärnur vanished. Aragorn Elessar took the crown in T.A. 3019 and his son Eldarion followed him.

places.note: Minas Tirith was the chief city of the later kings.
Osgiliath was the old capital before the Kin-strife.

sources: The Lord of the Rings, Appendix A (I, iv)

title: The Ruling Stewards of Gondor (list)
kind: List of the Ruling Stewards
blurb: The twenty-six Ruling Stewards of Gondor, from Mardil Voronwë to Denethor II.
book:
The Stewards were of the House of Húrin. After the last king vanished, they ruled in the name of the king who would one day return.

Mardil Voronwë, the Steadfast
Eradan
Herion
Belegorn
Húrin I
Túrin I
Hador
Barahir
Dior
Denethor I
Boromir
Cirion
Hallas
Húrin II
Belecthor I
Orodreth
Ecthelion I
Egalmoth
Beren
Beregond
Belecthor II
Thorondir
Túrin II
Turgon
Ecthelion II
Denethor II, last of the Ruling Stewards (died in T.A. 3019)

Cirion gave Calenardhon to Eorl in the time of the Oath of Cirion. After the War of the Ring, Faramir served as Steward under King Elessar.

places.note: The Stewards ruled from Minas Tirith.

sources: The Lord of the Rings, Appendix A (II)

title: The Kings of Rohan (list)
kind: List of the Kings of the Mark
blurb: The kings of Rohan in three lines, from Eorl the Young to Éomer Éadig.
book:
Eorl the Young led the Éothéod south and received Calenardhon from Cirion in T.A. 2510. The Kings of the Mark follow in three lines.

First line: Eorl the Young (killed in battle in the Wold, T.A. 2545)
Brego
Aldor the Old, third son of Brego (his elder brother Baldor was lost on the Paths of the Dead)
Fréa
Fréawine
Goldwine
Déor
Gram
Helm Hammerhand
Second line: Fréaláf Hildeson, nephew of Helm
Brytta Léofa
Walda
Folca
Folcwine
Fengel
Thengel
Théoden, slain on the Pelennor Fields
Third line: Éomer Éadig, nephew of Théoden

Wulf of Dunland usurped the throne for a time during the Long Winter. Fréaláf slew him and began the second line. Théoden's son Théodred fell at the Fords of Isen, so his sister's son Éomer became king.

places.note: Edoras was the royal seat of the Kings of the Mark.

sources: The Lord of the Rings, Appendix A (II)

title: The Kings of Durin's Folk (list)
kind: Line of the Dwarf-kings of Durin's Folk
blurb: The heirs of Durin the Deathless, from Khazad-dûm to Erebor and the Iron Hills.
book:
Durin the Deathless woke first of the seven Fathers and founded Khazad-dûm. His line kept the title of King of Durin's Folk through many ages.

Durin the Deathless, the Father of Durin's Folk
Many kings called Durin and others followed in Khazad-dûm; the books do not list them all
Durin VI, slain by the Balrog (Durin's Bane) in T.A. 1980
Náin I, slain by the Balrog soon after
Thráin I, son of Náin I, who founded the realm of Erebor in T.A. 1999
Thorin I, who moved the court to the Grey Mountains in T.A. 2210
Glóin
Óin
Náin II
Dáin I, slain by a cold-drake with his son Frór
Thrór, who returned to Erebor and lost it to Smaug
Thráin II, son of Thrór, captive in Dol Guldur
Thorin II Oakenshield, slain in the Battle of Five Armies (T.A. 2941)
Dáin II Ironfoot, grandson of Grór son of Dáin I, lord of the Iron Hills and then King under the Mountain
Thorin III Stonehelm, son of Dáin II

Thrór held the last of the Seven Rings kept by Durin's line. Thráin II bore it until it was taken from him in Dol Guldur.

places.note: Durin's heirs held Khazad-dûm until the Balrog.
Thráin I founded the kingdom under the Mountain at Erebor.

sources: The Lord of the Rings, Appendix A (III)
The Hobbit, chapter 1

title: The Kings under the Mountain and the Kings of Dale (list)
kind: Lists of the rulers of Erebor and Dale
blurb: The kings of Erebor and the lords and kings of Dale, from Thráin I to the Reunited Kingdom.
book:
Erebor and Dale stood close together and were friends. The Dwarves of Durin's line ruled the Mountain, and Men ruled the town below it.

Under the Mountain: Thráin I, who founded the realm in T.A. 1999
Thorin I, who left for the Grey Mountains
Thrór, who returned to Erebor in T.A. 2590 and lost it to Smaug in T.A. 2770
Thorin II Oakenshield, who regained the Mountain and was slain in T.A. 2941
Dáin II Ironfoot (T.A. 2941 to 3019)
Thorin III Stonehelm
Dale: Girion, Lord of Dale when Smaug came
Bard the Bowman (Bard I), who slew Smaug and became King of Dale
Bain, son of Bard
Brand, son of Bain, slain in the battle at Dale in T.A. 3019
Bard II, son of Brand

Dale was ruined by Smaug. Bard rebuilt it in T.A. 2944. The kings of Erebor and Dale stood together in the War of the Ring. Dáin and Brand both died in the battle at Dale in T.A. 3019.

places.note: The Kings under the Mountain ruled Erebor.
The lords and kings of Dale ruled the town below the Mountain.

sources: The Lord of the Rings, Appendix A (III)
The Hobbit, chapters 12 to 18

title: The Baggins family (family line)
kind: Family line of Bilbo and Frodo
blurb: The Baggins family of Hobbiton, from Balbo to Bilbo and Frodo, with the Sackville-Bagginses as cousins.
book:
The Bagginses were a respectable Hobbit family of Hobbiton and Bag End. Two of them carried the One Ring.

Balbo Baggins and his wife Berylla Boffin
Mungo Baggins, son of Balbo
Bungo Baggins, son of Mungo, who built Bag End and married Belladonna Took
Bilbo Baggins, son of Bungo and Belladonna, born in S.R. 1290
Longo Baggins, another son of Mungo, married Camellia Sackville; their son was Otho Sackville-Baggins
Largo Baggins, another son of Balbo, father of Fosco
Drogo Baggins, son of Fosco
Drogo and Primula Brandybuck: Frodo Baggins, born in S.R. 1368
Drogo and Primula both drowned in the Brandywine
Bilbo adopted Frodo and made him his heir
Otho Sackville-Baggins and Lobelia Bracegirdle: Lotho

Bilbo and Frodo were cousins on both sides. This list leaves out many members of the family. Bilbo left Bag End in S.R. 1401. Frodo sold it to the Sackville-Bagginses and left in S.R. 1418.
sources: The Lord of the Rings, Prologue and Appendix C
The Hobbit, chapter 1

title: The Took family and the Thains (family line)
kind: Family line of the Thains of the Shire
blurb: The Took family, leaders of the Shire as Thains, with a partial list of the Thains.
book:
The Thain was the master of the Shire-moot and the captain of the Shire-muster and the hobbitry-in-arms. The title belonged first to the Oldbuck family and then to the Took family.

Bucca of the Marish, first Thain, in S.R. 379, head of the Oldbucks
The Oldbucks held the title for twelve Thains in all
Isumbras I, thirteenth Thain and the first of the Took line, in S.R. 740
Isengrim II, Thain, who began the Great Smials in S.R. 1083
Bandobras Took, called Bullroarer, of Isengrim's line (the Prologue calls him a son of Isengrim II; the family tree in Appendix C makes him a grandson), who beat the goblin chief Golfimbul at Greenfields in S.R. 1147; he was not Thain
Gerontius Took, the Old Took, Thain, who lived to the age of 130
The Old Took's children included Belladonna, mother of Bilbo, and Mirabella, grandmother of Frodo
Paladin II, Thain at the time of the War of the Ring
Peregrin I (Pippin), son of Paladin II, Thain from S.R. 1434
Faramir I, son of Peregrin, who married Goldilocks, daughter of Sam Gamgee

The Tooks lived at Tuckborough and in the Great Smials. Some Tooks were adventurous, and this ran in the blood of Belladonna and her son Bilbo. This list is not complete. It leaves out many Thains between Isumbras I and Paladin II.
sources: The Lord of the Rings, Prologue and Appendix C
The Lord of the Rings, Appendix B

title: The Brandybuck family and the Masters of Buckland (family line)
kind: Family line of the Masters of Buckland
blurb: The Brandybucks, who ruled Buckland, with a partial list of their Masters.
book:
The Brandybucks lived at Brandy Hall in Buckland. Their head held the title Master of Buckland.

Gorhendad Oldbuck, head of the Oldbucks, who crossed the Brandywine about S.R. 740, began Brandy Hall and changed his name to Brandybuck
Gormadoc Deepdelver Brandybuck, in a later generation
Gorbadoc Broadbelt, husband of Mirabella Took, father of Rorimac and Primula
Primula Brandybuck, wife of Drogo Baggins and mother of Frodo
Rorimac Goldfather, called Old Rory, Master of Buckland, husband of Menegilda Goold
Saradoc Scattergold, son of Rorimac, who married Esmeralda Took
Meriadoc the Magnificent (Merry), son of Saradoc, Master of Buckland from S.R. 1432

Buckland lay east of the Brandywine and was almost a country of its own. Frodo spent his youth at Brandy Hall. The Old Forest and the Hedge shielded Buckland. This list is not complete.
sources: The Lord of the Rings, Prologue, 'Of the Ordering of the Shire'
The Lord of the Rings, Appendix C

title: The Gamgee and Cotton families (family line)
kind: Family lines of Sam Gamgee and Rose Cotton
blurb: The Gamgee and Cotton families of Hobbiton and Bywater, and the thirteen children of Sam and Rose.
book:
The Gamgees came of a family of ropemakers, and the Gaffer and Sam were gardeners. The Cottons farmed near Bywater.

Hamfast Gamgee, called the Gaffer, gardener at Bag End
The Gaffer and his wife Bell Goodchild had six children: Hamson, Halfred, Daisy, May, Samwise and Marigold
Samwise Gamgee, born in S.R. 1380, later Mayor of the Shire
Tolman Cotton (Farmer Cotton), father of Rose
Rose Cotton, who married Sam in S.R. 1420
Sam and Rose's children: Elanor, Frodo, Rose, Merry, Pippin, Goldilocks, Hamfast, Daisy, Primrose, Bilbo, Ruby, Robin and Tolman
Elanor the Fair, who became a maid of honour to Queen Arwen and married Fastred of Greenholm

Sam kept the Red Book after Frodo and handed it to Elanor when he went to the Grey Havens. Elanor kept the book at Undertowers after Sam sailed West.
sources: The Lord of the Rings, Appendix B and Appendix C
The Lord of the Rings, Book VI, chapter 9

title: The Fellowship of the Ring (list)
kind: List of the nine Walkers
blurb: The nine members of the Fellowship, each with the people it stood for and what became of it.
book:
Elrond chose nine Walkers to set against the nine Black Riders. They left Rivendell in T.A. 3018.

Frodo Baggins, a Hobbit: Ring-bearer, who bore the Ring to Mount Doom and sailed West in S.R. 1421
Samwise Gamgee, a Hobbit: companion of Frodo, who later became Mayor of the Shire and sailed West in S.R. 1482
Meriadoc Brandybuck, a Hobbit: later Master of Buckland, who died in Gondor
Peregrin Took, a Hobbit: later Thain of the Shire, who also died in Gondor
Gandalf, a Wizard and Maia, who left Middle-earth in S.R. 1421
Aragorn, a Man of the Dúnedain: later King Elessar of Gondor and Arnor
Boromir, a Man of Gondor: slain at Amon Hen
Legolas, an Elf of the Woodland Realm: who later sailed West
Gimli, a Dwarf of Durin's Folk: who sailed West with Legolas

Merry and Pippin were laid to rest near Aragorn in Rath Dínen. Legolas and Gimli left Middle-earth after the death of Aragorn in the Fourth Age. The party broke up at Parth Galen after Boromir's death.
sources: The Lord of the Rings, Book II, chapter 3
The Lord of the Rings, Book VI, chapter 9
The Lord of the Rings, Appendix A and B

title: Thorin's company (list)
kind: List of the thirteen Dwarves
blurb: The thirteen Dwarves who went with Bilbo to Erebor, with their kinship and what became of each.
book:
Thorin led twelve Dwarves and the hobbit Bilbo to the Lonely Mountain in T.A. 2941. Gandalf set the quest in motion.

Thorin Oakenshield, leader, son of Thráin II; slain in the Battle of Five Armies
Fíli and Kíli, sons of Thorin's sister Dís; both fell defending Thorin
Balin and Dwalin, sons of Fundin and kin to Thorin; Balin later led a colony in Moria and fell there in T.A. 2994
Óin and Glóin, brothers and sons of Gróin; Óin went with Balin and died in Moria, Glóin lived and fathered Gimli
Dori, Nori and Ori; Ori went with Balin and died in Moria
Bifur, Bofur and Bombur, who came of Moria Dwarves but not of Durin's line; Bombur grew very fat in later years

Dwalin and several of the others lived long after the quest. Gandalf chose Bilbo as the burglar so that the company would not number thirteen. The books do not tell the fate of every Dwarf in full.

facts.Goal: Erebor and the treasure of Smaug

sources: The Hobbit, chapters 1 and 18
The Lord of the Rings, Appendix A (III)
The Fellowship of the Ring, Book II, chapter 5
Unfinished Tales, Part Three, The Quest of Erebor

title: The bearers of the One Ring (list)
kind: List of the Ring's keepers, with years
blurb: The people who held the One Ring from its forging until its destruction, in order.
book:
Sauron made the One Ring in the Second Age. Several others held it before it was destroyed in Mount Doom.

Sauron, maker of the Ring, who forged it about S.A. 1600
Isildur, who cut the Ring from Sauron's hand in S.A. 3441 and lost it in the Anduin in T.A. 2
Déagol, who found it in the river about T.A. 2463
Sméagol, later called Gollum, who took it from Déagol and kept it for nearly five hundred years
Bilbo Baggins, who found it in the Misty Mountains in T.A. 2941
Frodo Baggins, to whom Bilbo gave it in T.A. 3001
Samwise Gamgee, who held it for a short time in Mordor

Gollum took the Ring again at Mount Doom and fell with it into the fire on 25 March, T.A. 3019. Frodo kept the Ring from T.A. 3001 and was named Ring-bearer at the Council of Elrond in T.A. 3018. Tom Bombadil and Gandalf also handled it briefly in 3018.
sources: The Lord of the Rings, Book I, chapter 2
The Lord of the Rings, Book VI, chapter 3
The Silmarillion, Of the Rings of Power

title: The keepers of the Three Rings (list)
kind: List of the holders of Narya, Nenya and Vilya
blurb: The holders of the Three Rings of the Elves, in order for each ring.
book:
Celebrimbor made the three Elven Rings without Sauron's help. They were kept hidden and never touched by Sauron.

Narya, the Ring of Fire: Celebrimbor, then Gil-galad, then Círdan, then Gandalf
Nenya, the Ring of Water: Celebrimbor, then Galadriel
Vilya, the Ring of Air: Celebrimbor, then Gil-galad, then Elrond

Celebrimbor made the Rings in Eregion. Narya and Vilya went to Gil-galad and Nenya to Galadriel. Gil-galad later passed Narya to Círdan and Vilya to Elrond. Círdan gave Narya to Gandalf at the Grey Havens. When the One Ring was destroyed, the Three lost their power and the bearers sailed West.

facts.Status: Power ended with the One Ring (T.A. 3019)

sources: The Silmarillion, Of the Rings of Power
The Lord of the Rings, Appendix B

title: The seven palantíri (list)
kind: List of the seven seeing-stones
blurb: The seven palantíri of the Dúnedain: where each stood and what became of each.
book:
The palantíri were seeing-stones made by the Noldor in Valinor. Elendil brought seven to Middle-earth. They let the viewer see far places.

Osgiliath: the great stone of Gondor, lost in the Anduin during the Kin-strife
Minas Anor (Minas Tirith): the Anor-stone, kept in the White Tower
Minas Ithil: the Ithil-stone, taken by Sauron when Minas Ithil fell
Orthanc: the stone of Isengard, used by Saruman, whom Sauron ensnared through it
Amon Sûl: the chief stone of the North, later kept at Fornost and lost with Arvedui
Annúminas: also lost with them
Elostirion: the Elostirion stone on the Tower Hills, which looks only West

King Arvedui carried the two northern stones in his ship. They sank in the Ice Bay of Forochel in T.A. 1975. Denethor looked into the Anor-stone and was driven to despair by Sauron. After Gríma threw the Orthanc-stone down from the tower, Aragorn claimed it.
sources: The Lord of the Rings, Book III, chapter 11 and Appendix A
Unfinished Tales, Part Four, chapter 3

title: The Valar (list)
kind: List of the fourteen Valar and their realms
aka: Lords and Queens of the West
blurb: The fourteen Valar, seven Lords and seven Queens, with the realm of each.
book:
The Valar are the great Powers of Arda, sent by Ilúvatar to shape and guard the world. Seven are called Lords and seven Queens.

Manwë: lord of air and winds, King of Arda; wife of Varda
Ulmo: lord of all waters
Aulë: smith and maker, lord of earth and crafts; husband of Yavanna
Oromë: hunter and lord of forests; husband of Vána
Mandos (Námo): keeper of the Halls of the dead and giver of doom; husband of Vairë
Irmo (Lórien): lord of dreams, visions and gardens; husband of Estë
Tulkas: the strong, a wrestler and champion; husband of Nessa
Varda: queen of the stars and light
Yavanna: giver of fruits, lady of growing things
Nienna: lady of pity and mourning
Estë: lady of healing and rest
Vairë: weaver of the tales of time
Vána: queen of flowers and spring
Nessa: lady of dance and deer

Melkor was once counted among the Valar, but he turned to evil and is not named in this list. Mandos and Irmo are brothers, and Nienna is their sister.
sources: The Silmarillion, Valaquenta

title: The seven sons of Fëanor (list)
kind: List of Fëanor's sons and their fates
blurb: The seven sons of Fëanor and Nerdanel, with the fate of each.
book:
Fëanor and his seven sons swore an oath to win back the Silmarils. The oath drove them to the Kinslayings and ruin.

Maedhros the Tall, eldest: captive of Morgoth, freed by Fingon, later took a Silmaril and cast himself into a chasm
Maglor the singer: cast his Silmaril into the sea, then wandered the shores; his end is not told
Celegorm the Fair: slain by Dior in Doriath
Caranthir the Dark: slain in Doriath
Curufin the Crafty: slain in Doriath, father of Celebrimbor
Amrod and Amras, the twins: perished at the Havens of Sirion

Only Maedhros and Maglor lived to the end of the First Age. The Silmarils were lost to them. Some of Tolkien's later notes give different details for Amrod and Amras.
sources: The Silmarillion, chapters 5, 22, 24

title: Named swords and weapons (list)
kind: List of named arms and their bearers
blurb: The named weapons of Middle-earth and the people who bore them.
book:
Many blades and bows in Tolkien's tales have their own names. This list gathers the best known and the people who bore them.

Narsil, made by Telchar, borne by Elendil; shards later reforged as Andúril
Andúril, borne by Aragorn
Glamdring, found in the Troll's hoard by Gandalf; made in Gondolin
Orcrist, found with Glamdring, borne by Thorin Oakenshield
Sting, found by Bilbo, who later gave it to Frodo; Sam also carried it in Cirith Ungol
Anglachel, later reforged as Gurthang, borne by Beleg and then Túrin
Anguirel, the twin sword of Anglachel, kept by Eöl and taken by Maeglin
Ringil, sword of Fingolfin
Aeglos, spear of Gil-galad
Angrist, knife of Curufin
Belthronding, bow of Beleg
Black Arrow, an heirloom of Bard's line, shot by Bard at Smaug
Guthwinë, sword of Éomer
Herugrim, sword of Théoden
Barrow-blades, carried by the Hobbits from the barrow of Cardolan

Glamdring and Orcrist glow when Orcs are near. Telchar the smith of Nogrod made Narsil, and Isildur cut the Ring from Sauron's hand with the hilt-shard of Narsil.

facts.Reforged: Narsil became Andúril in T.A. 3018, before the Fellowship left Rivendell

sources: The Silmarillion
The Lord of the Rings
The Hobbit
